name: Deep Glaucous-Green
lede: Deep Glaucous-Green is a soft, dusty green from Ridgway's 1912 chart, named for the pale bluish bloom botanists call glaucous, like the waxy coating on a cabbage leaf or a plum.

sections.title: A botanist's word for a bloom
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 plate XXXIII gives this hue the name Deep Glaucous-Green, hue 39′′, tone b, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files the nearest category as "light green" in its block 144 [1]. *Glaucous* is a botanical term for the dull, waxy, bluish-grey bloom on leaves, stems and fruit, such as a cabbage or a plum, and Ridgway used the word across a run of greens and blues on his chart [1]. A lighter [[dark-bluish-glaucous]] and a plainer [[morning-blue]] sit nearby in our name list, part of the same family [1].

In LCH terms it measures lightness 71, chroma 18, hue 145 degrees, Munsell 0.9G 7.0/2.7 [1]. Its closest match in the library is [[cameo-green]], about 2.9 CIEDE2000 units away, with [[rejane-green]] close behind at 3.4 units [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A match within six CIEDE2000 units covering at least five percent of the canvas turns up in 134 of our 23,781 archive paintings, about 0.56 percent, as photographed [4]. It peaks in the 1770s, in 8 of 416 paintings, at 3.4 times the overall rate, and is most loved by Vincent van Gogh, in five of his forty-nine paintings here, eighteen times his own museums' baseline; it most often plays a highlight, in 81 percent of its appearances [4].

The earliest dated match is Sandro Botticelli's *The Triumph of Mordecai*, 1475, more than four centuries before Ridgway recorded the name in 1912; early centuries are thin in the archive, so this is a floor, not a first, and a photograph of an aged canvas is a screen color, not a pigment test [4].
